newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-S.African transfers mark Super 12 buildup.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-S.African transfers mark Super 12 buildup.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Feb 27 - Significant player movement between provinces reflects a far greater preparation by South Africa teams than last season for the second Super 12 rugby series starting this weekend, reports Harris Choy of NZPA.
Player revolt ousted John Williams from his coaching job at North Transvaal, who now have another Springbok mentor, Kitch Christie, at the helm.
His deputy Uli Schmidt was a highly competitive Springbok hooker until 1995.

Springbok James Small, who claims to be the only winger to have stopped the colossal Jonah Lomu in full flight, has switched from last year's Super 12 finalists Natal to Western Province. Western Province lost their Super 12 spot this year to Free State.
Phillip Schutte, a Springbok lock in 1994 has also switched to Western Province from Transvaal.
Natal have gained Transvaal fullback Gavin Lawless, top points scorer on the South African scene last season, and lock Wayne Boardman.

Among them: Auckland's Zinzan Brooke, Michael Jones, Andrew Blowers, the Hurricanes' Christian Cullen, Canterbury's Andrew Mehrtens, Natal's Andre Joubert, Transvaal's James Dalton and Chris Rossouwe and Queensland's Jason Little.
New Zealand heavyweights Auckland have also lost Jonah Lomu to a kidney disorder.

Two unexpected developments in the first season of the professional competition in 1996 were the demise of the Pienaar-led Transvaal and the emergence of ACT, a patchwork quilt side, made in part from NSW and Queensland offcuts.

Sadly, missing from the South African scene this season will be 1995 World Cup captain Francois Pienaar (Saracens), Transvaal's influential leader, his Springboks team mate Rudolph Streuli (Bedford), Hannes Venter (playing league), Steve Atherton (Richmond), Argentinian prop Diego Mendez (Bath), Joel Stransky (Leicester) and French international Thierry Lacroix (Harlequins).

The impact of last season's thrilling, high-speed and often ferocious Super 12 and tri-series, easily the most gruelling season experienced by all three nations involved, left a long list of casualties.
Pre-competition, the Brumbies were maligned in South Africa and New Zealand, dismissed as easybeats who would not win a game. They almost made the semifinals, and Australia found a third rugby power.
Nevertheless, Australia's and South Africa's national and provincial teams were beaten black and blue by New Zealand.

While New Zealand rugby brains such as John Hart and Grant Fox are more cautious about South African teams this year, Australian and South African experts believe the scenario won't be too different this seasos.
The All Blacks and Auckland Blues claimed the tri nations and Super 12 series respectively last year with a brand of running rugby that stunned their opponents.

Queensland were perhaps the only side to beat Auckland at their own game, inflicting a stunning 51-13 upset at Ballymore, but the Blues, averaging almost 40 points a game, eventually cruised to the inaugural title.
With 13 All Blacks in the squad, they made the semifinal against Northern Transvaal and the final against Natal almost no-contests.
CentreBet in Alice Springs has Auckland at 13-8 to win back-to-back titles, with Natal at 9-4, Transvaal at 7-1 and Queensland and Northern Transvaal the only other teams under double figures at 8-1.

Love them or hate them, the delight of the Super 12 were the Zinzan Brooke-led Aucklanders. Their powerful forwards fringed with robust flankers Charles Reichelmann and Blowers, the sweet skills of Brooke, the efficient spadework of their front rowers including Olo Brown and Sean Fitzpatrick and the cutting edge of their backs from the talented first five-eighth Carlos Spencer to storming wingers Jonah Lomu and Joeli Vidiri churned out a brand new game.
Lomu will miss the competition but Auckland have found a more experienced and sharper replacement in Samoan international Brian Lima.
"In terms of pure talent you can't go much past Auckland as the favourite," according to former Wallaby Grand Slam captain and now Queensland assistant coach Andrew Slack.
Andre Markgraaff, who quit as Springboks coach last week following his racial remarks, said Australian teams should be watched closely.
"The New Zealanders use the whole field and defensively you're up against it because they will run it from everywhere and what's more they have the skill to do it," he said.
"But Australia's headed that way and NSW especially are very well prepared in terms of fitness and I think they will be able to measure up in terms of running the ball from any part of the field.
Hart believes South Africans teams will be even harder this season as they will be far better prepared.

Natal, last year's beaten finalist, would be the best of the South African provinces with a host of national players including No 8 Gary Teichmann, second-rower Mark Andrews and Joubert when he has recovered from injury.
Northern Transvaal, with their rock-like defence and dynamic halfback Joost van der Westhuizen, should at least go close to repeating their semifinal appearance of last year.
Queensland, unbeaten at home last season contain nearly a fully quota of Wallabies.

New South Wales, brilliant but frustratingly inconsistent in last season would provide the greatest challenge with an attacking weapon of such calibre as Wallaby fullback Matt Burke and a favourable draw with six of 11 matches at home.
No doubt each side recognises the importance of winning away from home -- a feat achieved just 20 times in 69 matches last year. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
